column1: How many phonemic vowels does Spanish have, and what are they?
column2: Five vowels: /i, e, a, o, u/ — high front /i/, mid front /e/, low central /a/, mid back /o/, high back /u/, forming a symmetrical pentagonal vowel space.

column1: What phonological process causes /θ/ to merge with /s/, and where is it common?
column2: Seseo — the merger of /θ/ and /s/ into a single /s/ sound, characteristic of Latin American Spanish and parts of southern Spain (Andalusia), contrasting with Peninsular Castilian distinción.

column1: Decompose the Spanish verb form 'trabajábamos' into its morphological components.
column2: trabaj- (root 'work') + -a- (thematic vowel, 1st conjugation marker) + -ba- (imperfect tense-aspect marker) + -mos (1st person plural agreement) — illustrating rightward cumulative exponence.

column1: What three grammatical dimensions does the Spanish verbal system encode simultaneously?
column2: Tense (temporal location), Aspect (bounded/perfective vs. unbounded/imperfective internal structure), and Mood (indicative realis vs. subjunctive irrealis vs. imperative).

column1: What is the core semantic difference between preterite and imperfect aspect, independent of objective event duration?
column2: Preterite presents an event as a closed, bounded whole viewed from outside (foreground, plot-advancing); imperfect presents it as an open, unbounded process viewed from inside (background, scene-setting) — aspect reflects speaker framing, not real-world duration.

column1: In narrative Spanish, what distinct discourse functions do preterite and imperfect verbs serve?
column2: Preterite verbs advance the narrative timeline by asserting new completed events (foreground/figure); imperfect verbs freeze the timeline to describe ongoing states or habitual backdrops (background/ground).

column1: What is the pro-drop parameter, and why does Spanish license it?
column2: The pro-drop parameter allows phonetically null subject pronouns (represented as 'pro') because rich verbal agreement morphology recovers person/number features, e.g., 'Habla francés' unambiguously implies él/ella/usted as subject.

column1: List three syntactic phenomena that correlate with Spanish's pro-drop status.
column2: 1) Null subjects (pro), 2) free subject-verb inversion (Llegó María / María llegó), 3) expletive-less weather predicates (Llueve vs. English 'It rains').

column1: What does Differential Object Marking (DOM) in Spanish mark, and what is its key exponent?
column2: DOM uses the preposition 'a' before animate and/or specific direct objects, encoding an intersection of animacy, referential specificity, and pragmatic topicality (e.g., 'Vi a María' vs. 'Vi el libro').

column1: What grammatical function does clitic doubling serve beyond redundancy in Spanish?
column2: It is a grammaticalized information-packaging device signaling definiteness, discourse prominence, and affectedness hierarchies when a full noun phrase co-occurs with a corresponding pronominal clitic.

column1: What major sound change explains why Spanish 'hablar' has a silent 'h' where Latin had an 'f' (as in 'fabulare')?
column2: The sound shift f > h > ∅: initial Latin /f/ weakened to /h/ (aspirated) and eventually dropped entirely in most dialects, leaving a silent orthographic 'h'.

column1: How did Vulgar Latin's case system transform into modern Spanish's grammatical encoding strategy?
column2: Vulgar Latin eroded the six-case nominal paradigm toward a two-case remnant and then to a caseless system; Spanish compensates by encoding grammatical relations through fixed word order and prepositions instead of noun-ending inflection.
